title: How we estimate, and the data
summary.title: The model in brief (VPH-1.1)
summary.pool: We rebuild, month by month, the national line of pending Cuban I-485s from the USCIS monthly reports since {month}.
summary.beta: Each month USCIS decides some number of cases. The model spreads those decisions over the pending cases; older cases have a small advantage ({beta} per month of age).
summary.scenarios: No one knows how many cases USCIS will decide in the future, so we mix four policy scenarios with weights that are updated with new data and reviewed alerts.
summary.conditioning: Then we compute the chance of a decision within each horizon for a case that is still pending today.
summary.holds: Adjudication holds (R1 and R3) do not count as adjudicable time.
summary.group: It is the national average for Cuban I-485s, not a prediction for any one case, and we always show it with ranges.
bias.title: Why the published numbers mislead
bias.completionOnly: Only finished cases count: in {month} there were {n} decisions among {pending} pending, so published times describe only {share} of the files.
bias.selection: During a hold, the few cases that finish are not typical (clear denials, abandoned files). That is why the approval share fell without any change in the group's eligibility.
bias.immortal: Counting from the filing date includes months when USCIS could not decide because of the holds. That is why we show adjudicable days.
bias.regimeLag: A calculation based on past cases keeps predicting the past when policy changes.
bias.aggregation: Office data mixes Cubans with refugees and asylees, and the USCIS time is for the family-based I-485, not Cuban Adjustment. We use them only as relative indexes.
bias.reportingLag: USCIS publishes the monthly report 4 to 8 weeks after the month ends, and the quarterly one about 10 weeks after the quarter. That is why we always show the date of the data.

limits.title: Known limitations
limits.mixedPool: The national group mixes different cases (CHNV, CBP One, visas, problem cases). The model does not know which kind USCIS decides first; that is why we show a structural band next to the estimate.
limits.stateMixture: If we know your state but not your office, we mix the state's offices by their pending cases. That mix barely changes with how long your case has waited, even though a case pending many months is less likely to be at a fast office (a version 1 limitation).
limits.officeProxy: Office data is approximate: it includes refugees and asylees, counts approvals only, and some quarters include holds.
limits.postInterview: For the time after the interview we use attorney reports (low confidence).
limits.unseen: The model does not see criminal history, prior orders or the officer's discretion.
limits.policy: Policy explains most of the uncertainty, and no data can anticipate a new hold.
validation.title: Validation and confidence
validation.not_validated: Not validated: there are not yet enough months of the current regime to check the model.
validation.validated_r0r2: Validated only on the periods without holds (R0 and R2), not on the current regime.
validation.gates: Months of current-regime (R4) data: {months}. Confidence rises to medium with at least 6 months and checked forecasts.
validation.scorecard: The forecast scorecard arrives in version 1.1.
canary: Calculation check: with the {month} data, the example case gives a {p} chance of a decision within 12 months (median: {q50}). If this number changes without new data, something is wrong. Its ranges are on "My case".
